At the 1976 Summer Olympics in Montreal, reporters asked East German swimming coaches why their teenage female athletes suddenly had deep baritone voices and massive, heavily muscled shoulders.

The coaches laughed. They told the press they were in Montreal to swim, not to sing.

Newspapers printed the joke and moved on. When an American swimmer pointed out the obvious, that something in the pool wasn't right, sportswriters across the United States turned on her instead.

Her name was Shirley Babashoff.

She was nineteen years old, from Fountain Valley, California, and she had spent more than half her life preparing for that pool. Since the age of eight, she had trained under coach Mark Schubert at the Mission Viejo Nadadores club, waking up in the dark to swim ten thousand meters a day before and after high school.

At the 1972 Munich Games, she had won Olympic gold at fifteen. By 1976, holding multiple national records, she arrived in Montreal as the anchor of the American women's team.

Once the races began, the East German women dismantled every expectation in the aquatic center. They won eleven of the thirteen swimming gold medals and shattered world records in nearly every event.

Shirley swam the races of her life. She broke her own American records and walked away with four silver medals, posting times that would have guaranteed gold in almost any other era.

The American press expected her to smile on the podium and graciously congratulate the swimmers who beat her.

Shirley refused to play along. She stated plainly what everyone in the building could see: her competitors had developed deep voices and physiques unlike anything ever seen in women's swimming.

She wasn't media-trained, and she didn't hide her frustration when reporters pushed leading questions. She gave blunt answers and flatly refused to fake a smile for the cameras when she felt cheated on the world stage.

At the time, the International Olympic Committee had no reliable test to detect anabolic steroids, and Cold War politics prioritized keeping up the appearance of fair play. The United States Olympic Committee offered Shirley zero public defense.

American sportswriters found it far easier to attack an outspoken nineteen-year-old than to investigate an international sports machine. Columns across the country dubbed her "Surly Shirley," branding her a bitter runner-up and an embarrassment to American sportsmanship.

On the final day of the swimming events in Montreal, Shirley stepped onto the starting blocks for the 4×100-meter freestyle relay.

Her teammates, Kim Peyton, Wendy Boglioli, and Jill Sterkel, kept the race tight. When Shirley dove in for the anchor leg, she was swimming head-to-head against Kornelia Ender, the East German star who had already claimed four gold medals.

Shirley swam her leg in 55.48 seconds. The American women hit the wall in 3:44.82, beating East Germany by less than a second to win the gold medal.

It was the only women's swimming race the East Germans lost in the entire 1976 Olympics.

Even that victory couldn't shake the label the press had pinned on her. Shirley retired shortly after Montreal at nineteen years old, remembered by much of the public simply as the swimmer who complained.

Then, in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

In the early 1990s, the newly unified German government opened the archives of the Stasi, East Germany's secret police. Inside those files was a classified government directive called State Plan 14.25, a state-sponsored doping program engineered to prove communist superiority through Olympic medals.

The records laid out the exact milligrams of synthetic testosterone given to teenage girls. Doctors had handed thirteen- and fourteen-year-old swimmers little blue pills in locker rooms and at training tables, telling them they were vitamins. The pills were Oral-Turinabol, a potent anabolic steroid, administered in doses higher than those given to adult male weightlifters.

In the late 1990s, the doctors, coaches, and officials behind the program were put on trial in Berlin. Former East German athletes testified in court about failing livers, heart conditions, and severe birth defects in their children, victims of their own government.

Every allegation Shirley Babashoff had made in 1976 was proven as documented fact.

Still, the International Olympic Committee never changed the official record books, and the medals were never redistributed. Shirley went home to California, where she spent more than thirty years delivering mail for the United States Postal Service.
The 1976 times still stand.

She was asked to lose gracefully to a lie, and she chose to tell the truth even when her own country called her bitter for it. Why is it so often easier for people to punish the person pointing out an obvious unfairness than to confront the system behind it?

quote.author: HomerPavlos

quote.text:
There was a demographic problem 2,200 years ago, and Polybius wrote exactly what caused it. Read carefully:

"In our times, Greece as a whole is experiencing a lack of children and, more generally, a decrease in population. Because of this, cities have become deserted and there is a lack of productivity, even though we do not suffer from constant wars or epidemics. So if someone advised that we send priests to the gods to ask them what we should say or do to become more numerous and better inhabit our cities, he would not seem foolish, since the cause is obvious and the solution lies in our own hands.

People have turned to arrogance, greed, and laziness, and they neither want to marry, nor, if they do marry, to raise their children. Instead, they have only one or two children with difficulty, just to leave them wealth and raise them in luxury.

This evil grew rapidly, and we did not notice. For when there are only one or two children, and one is lost to war and the other to illness, it is obvious that the cities will inevitably become deserted, just as a beehive weakens little by little, so too do cities that lack population become unable to survive."

Source: Histories, Polybius, 36 (ΛΣΤ)

The similarities after 2,200 years.

The demographic issue has been a problem several times throughout history, and none of those times was it due to the economy, but rather a result of prosperity, comfortable living, and laziness. My Greek grandparents had children even when they had nothing to eat, and the kids grew up barefoot, eating bread with olives and feta cheese. Money was never an obstacle.

Nowadays, people prefer partying, doing drugs, and living for today rather than having a purpose, building a family, and leaving a positive footprint in this world. They choose the easy life. It’s sad watching people who passionately want to have kids but can’t, compared to people who don’t want kids because it would take them out of their comfort zone, because a child would stop them from going to clubs, drinking, and partying like a meaningless person.

- Homer Pavlos

Grok Build just got a solid upgrade for headless agents, MCP integrations, and remote terminal workflows

Headless sessions can now include images returned by MCP tools in streaming and JSON output, positional prompts automatically run headless when no interactive terminal is available, and local file links open directly from responses

Long-running headless tasks also get better reliability, with a five-minute inactivity timeout that prevents sessions from hanging indefinitely. Image pasting now works through remote tmux and nested terminal wrappers, while session recovery and hook inspection are more dependable

There’s also a performance improvement that eliminates unnecessary directory watching when Grok only needs to track the current Git branch

Release Notes: v1.0.92

Features:

• Positional prompts without `-p` now run headless and print their reply when the process has no terminal for the TUI
• MCP tool results that contain images now include those images in headless streaming and JSON output
• Clickable `file://` links to local files now open the file the same way bare paths do

Bug Fixes:

• Question cards in minimal mode now keep the first option visible instead of scrolling it off-screen
• Headless runs (`grok -p`) now stop after 5 minutes of no model output instead of hanging indefinitely
• Session resume errors now give the same helpful instruction on every route instead of suggesting the TUI picker
• `grok inspect` now shows the hooks a headless run would actually load, with a note for those that still need folder trust
• Image paste with `grok wrap` now works when Grok runs inside a remote tmux or through a second wrap

Performance:

• Grok no longer watches every directory when only tracking the current Git branch

"If printing money would end poverty, printing diplomas would end stupidity." Javier Milei.

This is France's problem in one sentence.

We did with degrees what central banks do with money: we printed them until they were worth nothing.

The master's degree has become a debased currency. And like all inflation, it leaves no visible victims. It quietly destroys the signal.

The result: average people, holding some forgettable master's from a second-rate university, sincerely believe they belong to the elite. They have the title. They have the stamp. They expect the status that's supposed to come with it. And when reality refuses to hand it over, they conclude the system is unfair.

But that's not even the real tragedy.

The real tragedy is that when everyone has the same degree, the degree says nothing. Truly brilliant people become invisible, drowned in a sea of identical CVs. We built a machine that makes mediocrity comfortable and excellence undetectable.

A country doesn't move forward because of how many graduates it produces. It moves forward because of a handful of exceptional people it knows how to spot, fund, and let build.

France doesn't need more graduates. It needs more brilliant people, recognized as brilliant for what they built, not for the paper on their wall.

Your degree says what you studied. What you built says who you are.

Printing diplomas never created intelligence. Only inflation.

"I have a real problem with people outside of our county trying to tell us what we should do and what we shouldn't do. My family goes back over since the eighteen eighties. I do not wanna ruin Cochise County. I do not wanna make it worse. In fact, that would be something that would horrify me."

"So, you know, the people at Cochise County, we're smart people. We know what we're doing. We know what we want for our vision, and we pass a comprehensive plan that's really thorough on everything. I would say to people, if you had the time like I did and went and checked each one of those signatures, you're gonna see that so many are not from Cochise County, like, at least 60% to even 70."

"So to me, I'm talking to the people on the street. I'm talking to the organizations that I meet, and that's where I'm gonna make my decision from what I hear from the people."

Elon Musk quickly impressed Franz von Holzhausen, persuading him to join Tesla and leave behind a successful career at Mazda. Franz recalls: "For somebody who's going to put rockets into space, car is actually not that hard, and his vision for the car and his sustainable direction and message is exactly what I'm looking for."

In the summer of 2008, Franz already had the kind of automotive career most designers dream about, having penned sports cars at GM and led design at Mazda North America, while Tesla was near bankruptcy. 

But after meeting Elon Musk at SpaceX and going for a drive together in an early Roadster while people on the street stopped to stare, Franz walked away from his secure job to start designing the Model S from a blank sheet of paper. When he later explained why he took that leap of faith into a startup with no guarantees, his answer came down to Elon's total commitment: "Tesla was all in."
